name: Least number k such that there are exactly n powerful numbers between k^2 and (k+1)^2.
comment: Pettigrew gives a(1)-a(6) in table 14. He conjectures that k exists for every n. Surprisingly, a(8) is greater than 10^6, but a(9)=524827. The Mathematica program creates all powerful numbers <= nMax by computing all products of the form x^2 y^3.
a(10) is greater than 10^8. - _Giovanni Resta_, May 11 2006
Shiu (1980) proved that infinitely many values of k exist for every n. Therefore this sequence is infinite. - _Amiram Eldar_, Jul 10 2020
reference: József Sándor, Dragoslav S. Mitrinovic and Borislav Crstici, Handbook of Number Theory I, Springer Science & Business Media, 2005, chapter VI, p. 226.
link: Donovan Johnson, Powerful numbers between k^2 and (k+1)^2
Steve Pettigrew, Sur la distribution de nombres speciaux consecutifs, M.Sc. Thesis, Univ. Laval, 2000.
P. Shiu, On the number of square-full integers between successive squares, Mathematika, Vol. 27, No. 2 (1980), pp. 171-178.
example: a(3) = 31 because 968, 972 and 1000 are between 961 and 1024.
mathematica: nMax=10^12; lst={}; Do[lst=Join[lst, i^3 Range[Sqrt[nMax/i^3]]^2], {i,nMax^(1/3)}]; lst=Union[lst]; n=0; k=1; Do[n0=k; While[lst[[k]]<j^2, k++ ]; n1=k; If[n1-n0-1==n, Print[{n,j-1}]; n++ ], {j,Sqrt[nMax]}]
author: _T. D. Noe_, May 09 2006
ext: a(8) and the previously known a(9) from _Giovanni Resta_, May 11 2006
